extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (professional scientists, naturalists, and educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used in reviewing scientific books and assessing scientific work/approaches (example: Mendelian vs biometric methods and a general history of science). Focuses on intellectual attitude, methodological exactness, mathematical/quantitative basis, scope, and audience suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific attitude — avoid partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit which derives satisfaction from the victory of one opinion over another should be swept from science; there is no place for the party system in science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers/authors and scientists should adopt an apologetic, self-critical attitude rather than triumphant dogmatism; avoid proclaiming conclusions as absolute truths and resist intellectual partisanship that values 'victory' over truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish discovery from interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no fixed criterion marking where discovery ends and interpretation begins; one must be careful not to define discovery as that about which there can be no doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, separate empirical findings (discovery) from the theoretical narratives built upon them (interpretation). Do not treat interpretive assertions as equivalent to primary facts; remain open to revising interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological exactness — units vs masses (Mendelian vs biometric approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mendelian approach treats material as uniform, dealing with 'units' and predicting outcomes at a glance; the biometrician records detailed variations and treats phenomena as 'masses'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a method's notion of 'exactness' is appropriate to the problem scale: neither enlarging the target (ideal uniformity) nor reducing it to unobservable points is wholly satisfactory. Evaluate whether claims of predictive power are warranted given the scale and limits of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance predictive success and detailed measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mendelians emphasize the ability to predict (success without detailed variability records); biometricians emphasize faithful record-keeping and measurement of deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good scientific evaluation values both predictive capability and rigorous quantitative record-keeping; do not favour prediction alone without adequate empirical documentation, nor documentation alone when predictive structure is evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of quantitative tests and mathematical framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The true test of every scientific theory is a quantitative test based on comparison of the mathematician's formulae with the experimenter's measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing theories or surveys of science, require explicit quantitative validation and the mathematical underpinnings of hypotheses. Popular descriptions that ignore the mathematical framework risk misleading the non-mathematical reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include major theoretical developments when surveying scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: A work tracing the progress of science should not omit important theories (example criticisms: omission of the phase rule, the second law of thermodynamics, and significant mathematical developments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys/history volumes should cover the principal conceptual and mathematical milestones relevant to the subject; omissions of major laws or fields (e.g., radium, thermodynamics, mathematical advances) give a onesided view and are significant defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope selection for survey works
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to trace scientific progress of a century in a single moderate-sized volume is probably an impossible task; it might be better to confine attention to earlier discoveries and sketch later developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the book's chosen scope is realistic and whether its selection of material leads to imbalance or misleading emphasis. Recommend narrower focus or clear limits rather than overambitious comprehensiveness that yields omission or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience suitability and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful popular/scientific volume should be readable and recall to specialists interesting points in other branches; a book of convenient size, readable style and reasonable price is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work's style, level, and organisation match its intended audience (specialists vs general readers). Readability, concision, and affordability are positive attributes for broad utility; specialists benefit from works that refresh awareness of other fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission requirements for announcements in Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements of births, marriages and deaths are inserted in the advertisement pages of 'Nature' at the rate for two lines of eighteen words; each additional line of nine words costs (specified amount). Orders should be accompanied by remittance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical procedural rule for contributors: adhere to specified word/line limits and pricing; include payment when submitting advertisement announcements to the journal office.
